9. Inverse Problems

CNRS & DMA, École Normale Supérieure

Chapter PDF · Complete book

Inverse problems seek to reconstruct a signal from measurements that blur, omit, or mix its values. Direct inversion can amplify noise or leave several signals indistinguishable, so reconstruction must incorporate assumptions about the unknown signal. We study how spectral and variational regularization stabilize inversion, derive error bounds for quadratic penalties, and develop methods for deconvolution, inpainting, and tomography.

The main references for this chapter are [23, 29, 19].

9.1 Regularization of Inverse Problems¶

We extend the convex regularization introduced in Chapter 8 to linear measurement operators.

We consider a bounded linear map Φ:S→H\Phi : \mathcal{S}\rightarrow \mathcal{H}Φ:S→H, where the signal space S\mathcal{S}S is a Hilbert space or, more generally, a Banach space. The data space H\mathcal{H}H is a Hilbert space.

The operator models acquisition: an unknown high-resolution signal f0∈Sf_0 \in \mathcal{S}f0​∈S gives rise to the noisy observation

y=Φf0+w∈Hy = \Phi f_0 + w \in \mathcal{H}y=Φf0​+w∈H

where w∈Hw \in \mathcal{H}w∈H represents acquisition noise. Here the noise is deterministic; we assume only that ∣ ⁣∣w∣ ⁣∣H|\!| w |\!|_\mathcal{H}∣∣w∣∣H​ is bounded.

An acquisition device records finitely many observations, so applications usually take H=RP\mathcal{H}=\mathbb{R}^PH=RP. The number PPP may be small relative to the desired reconstruction dimension.

For numerical implementation, we discretize the signal space as S=RN\mathcal{S}=\mathbb{R}^NS=RN, where NNN is the number of grid points. Usually the grid is much finer than the measurement set, so N≫PN \gg PN≫P.

Infinite-dimensional function spaces remain useful for modeling the unknown f0f_0f0​ and analyzing recovery, particularly when choosing the signal space S\mathcal{S}S.

Direct inversion may be impossible because Φ\PhiΦ is not injective or the data do not lie in its range. Even when an inverse exists on the range, it may have a large norm or be unbounded. Applying it to noisy data amplifies the perturbation: formally, Φ−1y=f0+Φ−1w\Phi^{-1}y=f_0+\Phi^{-1}wΦ−1y=f0​+Φ−1w.

We now give a few representative examples of forward operators Φ\PhiΦ.

Denoising.

The identity operator Φ=IdS\Phi=\mathrm{Id}_\mathcal{S}Φ=IdS​ with S=H\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{H}S=H gives the denoising problem studied in Chapters 7 and 8.

De-blurring and super-resolution.

For a general operator Φ\PhiΦ, recovering f0f_0f0​ requires both inversion and denoising. These goals often conflict because inversion amplifies noise.

For example, in deblurring, Φ\PhiΦ is a translation-invariant operator corresponding to low-pass filtering with a kernel hhh

Φf=f⋆h.(9.1)\Phi f = f \star h. \tag{9.1}Φf=f⋆h.(9.1)

A periodic model takes S=H=L2(Td)\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{H}=L^2(\mathbb{T}^d)S=H=L2(Td); see Proposition 2.3.

In practice, the blurred signal is sampled on a grid: Φf={(f⋆h)(xk)  ;  0⩽k<P}\Phi f = \left\{ (f \star h)(x_k) \;;\; 0 \leqslant k< P \right\}Φf={(f⋆h)(xk​);0⩽k<P}. Figure 9.1, middle, shows the resulting low-resolution image Φf0\Phi f_0Φf0​.

Inverting such operators is useful for increasing the resolution of digital photographs and videos.

Interpolation and inpainting.

Inpainting reconstructs missing pixels. We model the masking operation by an operator that is diagonal in the spatial domain:

(Φf)(x)={0ifx∈Ω,f(x)ifx∉Ω.(9.2)(\Phi f)(x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 0 \quad \text{if} \quad x \in \Omega,\\ f(x) \quad \text{if} \quad x \notin \Omega. \end{array} \right. \tag{9.2}(Φf)(x)={0ifx∈Ω,f(x)ifx∈/Ω.​(9.2)

Here Ω\OmegaΩ is the missing region, either a subset of [0,1]d[0,1]^d[0,1]d in the continuous model or a set of pixel indices in the discrete model.

Figure 9.1, right, shows an example of a damaged image Φf0\Phi f_0Φf0​.

Figure 9.1. Examples of forward operators in inverse problems.

Medical imaging.

Many medical imaging devices provide indirect access to the signal of interest, with acquisition processes that can be approximated by a linear operator Φ\PhiΦ.

For a tomographic scanner, the Radon transform models acquisition. The Fourier slice theorem relates these measurements to Fourier data along radial lines.

An idealized magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) model also uses partial Fourier measurements:

Φf={f^(x)  ;  x∈Ω}.(9.3)\Phi f= \left\{ \hat f(x) \;;\; x \in \Omega \right\} . \tag{9.3}Φf={f^​(x);x∈Ω}.(9.3)

Here Ω\OmegaΩ consists of radial lines for tomography or acquisition trajectories such as spirals for MRI.

Electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) also infer internal activity from measurements at sensors outside the sources. Abstractly, such a linearized model can be written as (Φf)(s)=∫K(s,x)f(x) dx(\Phi f)(s)=\int K(s,x)f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x(Φf)(s)=∫K(s,x)f(x)dx, where the kernel depends on the geometry and physical model. Unlike a simple image blur, this kernel need not be translation invariant.

Regression for supervised learning.

Linear supervised learning is closely related to the imaging problems studied here, although it uses different notation. Section 13.3 develops the connection between regression and inverse problems.

In statistical learning, the data are nnn pairs (xi,yi)i=1n(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n(xi​,yi​)i=1n​ with feature vectors xi∈Rpx_i \in \mathbb{R}^pxi​∈Rp. A linear prediction model has the form yi=⟨β, xi⟩y_i = \langle \beta,\,x_i\rangleyi​=⟨β,xi​⟩, with unknown parameter β∈Rp\beta\in \mathbb{R}^pβ∈Rp. Placing the vectors xix_ixi​ in the rows of X∈Rn×pX \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}X∈Rn×p gives the approximate system Xβ≈yX \beta\approx yXβ≈y. This corresponds to the inverse problem Φf=y\Phi f=yΦf=y under the substitutions Φ↦X\Phi \mapsto XΦ↦X and f↦βf \mapsto \betaf↦β, with dimensions (P,N)→(n,p)(P,N) \rightarrow (n,p)(P,N)→(n,p).

In statistical learning, the model need not be correctly specified, and the design matrix XXX is often random. Its sampling fluctuations must then be controlled as n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞.

Ridge regression estimates the parameter by solving the normalized problem

min⁡β  12n∣ ⁣∣Xβ−y∣ ⁣∣2+λ∣ ⁣∣β∣ ⁣∣2\underset{\beta}{\min}\; \frac{1}{2n}|\!| X \beta-y |\!|^2 + \lambda|\!| \beta |\!|^2βmin​2n1​∣∣Xβ−y∣∣2+λ∣∣β∣∣2

The corresponding empirical quantities are therefore 1nX∗X∼Φ∗Φ\frac{1}{n}X^*X \sim \Phi^*\Phin1​X∗X∼Φ∗Φ for the covariance and 1nX∗y∼Φ∗y\frac{1}{n}X^*y \sim \Phi^*yn1​X∗y∼Φ∗y for the data term.

For independent observations in fixed dimension and with suitable finite moments, these empirical quantities fluctuate around their expectations at order n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2. In growing dimension, the relevant norm bounds also depend on the dimension and tail assumptions.

9.2 Warmup: Oracle Linear Inversion¶

We first seek an oracle estimator among inversion methods that act diagonally in a fixed basis, allowing the gains to depend on the unknown clean signal. The optimization then separates into one scalar problem per coefficient. Later we will obtain such estimators from a single optimization problem on the signal space.

Assume that the forward operator is diagonal in an orthonormal basis (ψk)(\psi_k)(ψk​):

Φf=∑kφk⟨f, ψk⟩ ψk,\Phi f = \sum_k \varphi_k \langle f,\,\psi_k\rangle \, \psi_k,Φf=k∑​φk​⟨f,ψk​⟩ψk​,

where the coefficients φk\varphi_kφk​ typically represent attenuation.

The observation model is

Y=Φf0+wY = \Phi f_0 + wY=Φf0​+w

where www is Gaussian white noise with variance σ2\sigma^2σ2. In a real orthonormal basis, its coefficients are independent centered Gaussians. In a complex Fourier basis they still have mean zero and second moment σ2\sigma^2σ2, which suffices for the risk calculation below. We work in finite dimension; infinite-dimensional white noise requires a generalized random-process interpretation.

For instance, if (ψk)k(\psi_k)_k(ψk​)k​ is the Fourier basis, this corresponds to a deconvolution problem Φf=h⋆f\Phi f = h \star fΦf=h⋆f where h^k=φk\hat h_k = \varphi_kh^k​=φk​. We consider the same diagonal estimator f~\tilde{f}f~​ as in the denoising case:

f~≔∑kλk⟨Y, ψk⟩ ψk.\tilde{f} \coloneqq \sum_k \lambda_k \langle Y,\,\psi_k\rangle \, \psi_k.f~​:=k∑​λk​⟨Y,ψk​⟩ψk​.

We minimize the mean squared error with respect to λ\lambdaλ:

Ew∥f~−f0∥2=∑kE∣⟨f~−f0, ψk⟩∣2=∑kE∣λk(φkck+⟨w, ψk⟩)−ck∣2.\mathbb{E}_w \|\tilde{f} - f_0\|^2 = \sum_k \mathbb{E} \left| \langle \tilde{f} - f_0,\,\psi_k\rangle \right|^2 = \sum_k \mathbb{E} \left| \lambda_k (\varphi_k c_k + \langle w,\,\psi_k\rangle) - c_k \right|^2 .Ew​∥f~​−f0​∥2=k∑​E∣∣​⟨f~​−f0​,ψk​⟩∣∣​2=k∑​E∣λk​(φk​ck​+⟨w,ψk​⟩)−ck​∣2.

Writing ck=⟨f0,ψk⟩c_k=\langle f_0,\psi_k\rangleck​=⟨f0​,ψk​⟩ and using the zero mean and variance of the noise,

Ew∥f~−f0∥2=∑k∣ck∣2∣φkλk−1∣2+∣λk∣2σ2.\mathbb{E}_w \|\tilde{f} - f_0\|^2 = \sum_k |c_k|^2 | \varphi_k \lambda_k - 1 |^2 + |\lambda_k|^2 \sigma^2 .Ew​∥f~​−f0​∥2=k∑​∣ck​∣2∣φk​λk​−1∣2+∣λk​∣2σ2.

The optimal coefficient of the oracle estimator solves

min⁡λk∣ck∣2∣φkλk−1∣2+∣λk∣2σ2,\min_{\lambda_k} |c_k|^2 | \varphi_k \lambda_k - 1 |^2 + |\lambda_k|^2 \sigma^2 ,λk​min​∣ck​∣2∣φk​λk​−1∣2+∣λk​∣2σ2,

i.e., it satisfies

∣ck∣2φkˉ(φkλk−1)+σ2λk=0,|c_k|^2 \bar{\varphi_k} ( \varphi_k \lambda_k - 1 ) + \sigma^2 \lambda_k = 0,∣ck​∣2φk​ˉ​(φk​λk​−1)+σ2λk​=0,

which gives

λk=∣ck∣2φkˉ∣ck∣2∣φk∣2+σ2.\lambda_k = \frac{ |c_k|^2 \bar{\varphi_k} }{ |c_k|^2 |\varphi_k|^2 + \sigma^2 }.λk​=∣ck​∣2∣φk​∣2+σ2∣ck​∣2φk​ˉ​​.

For φk≠0\varphi_k \neq 0φk​=0 and ck≠0c_k\neq0ck​=0, the oracle gains approach direct inversion as the noise vanishes:

λk⟶1φkas σ→0.\lambda_k \longrightarrow \frac{1}{\varphi_k}\qquad\text{as }\sigma\to0.λk​⟶φk​1​as σ→0.

As σ\sigmaσ increases, inversion is attenuated. For a simple Fourier-domain example, let k⩾1k\geqslant 1k⩾1, ∣ck∣2=k−α|c_k|^2=k^{-\alpha}∣ck​∣2=k−α and φk=k−β/2\varphi_k=k^{-\beta/2}φk​=k−β/2, with α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0α,β>0. Then

9.3 Theoretical Study of Quadratic Regularization¶

We outline a standard approach to recovery guarantees in Hilbert spaces. The emphasis is on modeling assumptions expressed through source conditions, and on limitations of the squared-norm penalty, notably saturation of convergence rates and loss of components in ker⁡(Φ)\ker(\Phi)ker(Φ).

9.3.1 Singular Value Decomposition¶

Finite dimension.

We begin with the finite-dimensional case Φ∈RP×N\Phi \in \mathbb{R}^{P \times N}Φ∈RP×N so that S=RN\mathcal{S}=\mathbb{R}^NS=RN and H=RP\mathcal{H}=\mathbb{R}^PH=RP are Hilbert spaces.

In this case, the singular value decomposition (SVD) provides a precise description of the operator and of linear inversion.

Proof

Computing the SVD of a dense matrix Φ∈RN×N\Phi \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}Φ∈RN×N typically costs O(N3)O(N^3)O(N3) operations.

Compact operators.

The SVD extends to compact operators Φ:S→H\Phi : \mathcal{S}\rightarrow \mathcal{H}Φ:S→H between separable Hilbert spaces. Compactness means that ΦB1\Phi B_1ΦB1​ is relatively compact, where B1={s∈S  ;  ∣ ⁣∣s∣ ⁣∣⩽1}B_1= \left\{ s \in \mathcal{S} \;;\; |\!| s |\!|\leqslant 1 \right\}B1​={s∈S;∣∣s∣∣⩽1} is the unit ball. Equivalently, every sequence (Φsk)k(\Phi s_k)_k(Φsk​)k​ with sk∈B1s_k \in B_1sk​∈B1​ has a convergent subsequence. In infinite dimension, the identity operator Φ:S→S\Phi : \mathcal{S}\rightarrow \mathcal{S}Φ:S→S is not compact.

Equivalently, compact operators Φ\PhiΦ admit an expansion analogous to (9.4):

Φ=∑m=1+∞σm⟨ ⋅ ,vm⟩um(9.6)\Phi = \sum_{m=1}^{+\infty} \sigma_m \langle\,\cdot\,,v_m\rangle u_m \tag{9.6}Φ=m=1∑+∞​σm​⟨⋅,vm​⟩um​(9.6)

Here (um)(u_m)(um​) and (vm)(v_m)(vm​) are orthonormal systems in H\mathcal{H}H and S\mathcal{S}S, respectively, and the positive singular values decrease to zero; finite-rank operators give a finite sum.

Convergence in (9.6) holds in the operator norm induced by the norms on S\mathcal{S}S and H\mathcal{H}H

∣ ⁣∣Φ∣ ⁣∣L(S,H):=sup⁡∣ ⁣∣u∣ ⁣∣S⩽1∣ ⁣∣Φu∣ ⁣∣H.|\!| \Phi |\!|_{\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{H})} \mathrel{:=}\sup_{|\!| u |\!|_\mathcal{S}\leqslant 1}|\!| \Phi u |\!|_\mathcal{H}.∣∣Φ∣∣L(S,H)​:=∣∣u∣∣S​⩽1sup​∣∣Φu∣∣H​.

For a nonzero operator Φ\PhiΦ with the expansion (9.6), ∣ ⁣∣Φ∣ ⁣∣L(S,H)=σ1|\!| \Phi |\!|_{\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{H})}=\sigma_1∣∣Φ∣∣L(S,H)​=σ1​.

If only RRR singular values are positive, then Φ\PhiΦ has finite rank R=dim⁡(Im(Φ))R=\dim(\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}(\Phi))R=dim(Im(Φ)). Squared-norm regularization restricts the reconstruction to ker⁡(Φ)⊥\ker(\Phi)^\botker(Φ)⊥, a space of dimension RRR, so the problem reduces to finite dimension. Nonlinear methods can also recover components in ker⁡(Φ)\ker(\Phi)ker(Φ) under suitable priors; this is sometimes called super-resolution.

Between Hilbert spaces, compact operators are exactly the operator-norm limits of finite-rank operators. This approximation property need not hold for arbitrary Banach spaces, although the definition of compactness itself extends to them.

Examples include integral operators on L2(Ω)L^2(\Omega)L2(Ω) with a continuous kernel k(x,y)k(x,y)k(x,y) defined for (x,y)∈Ω×Ω(x,y) \in \Omega\times\Omega(x,y)∈Ω×Ω, where Ω\OmegaΩ is a compact subset of Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd or the torus Td\mathbb{T}^dTd:

(Φf)(x)=∫Ωk(x,y)f(y)dy(\Phi f)(x) = \int_{\Omega} k(x,y) f(y) \mathrm{d}y(Φf)(x)=∫Ω​k(x,y)f(y)dy

where dy\mathrm{d}ydy is the Lebesgue measure.

Convolution Φf=f⋆h\Phi f = f \star hΦf=f⋆h on Td=(R/2πZ)d\mathbb{T}^d=(\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z})^dTd=(R/2πZ)d generalizes (9.5). Its kernel k(x,y)=h(x−y)k(x,y) = h(x-y)k(x,y)=h(x−y) is translation invariant, and the Fourier functions qm(x)=(2π)−d/2eim⋅xq_m(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}e^{\mathrm{i}m\cdot x}qm​(x)=(2π)−d/2eim⋅x diagonalize the operator. Its singular values are σm=∣h^m∣\sigma_m=|\hat h_m|σm​=∣h^m​∣, where h^m=∫Tdh(x)e−im⋅x dx\hat h_m=\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}h(x)e^{-\mathrm{i}m\cdot x}\,\mathrm{d}xh^m​=∫Td​h(x)e−im⋅xdx denotes the convolution multiplier.

Pseudoinverse.

We first work in finite dimension, or more generally assume that Im(Φ)\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}(\Phi)Im(Φ) is closed. Even without noise, Φf=y\Phi f=yΦf=y may be inconsistent, and a nontrivial kernel makes a solution nonunique. The Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse selects the least-squares solution of minimum norm

In infinite dimension, a compact operator of infinite rank has nonclosed range. Its pseudoinverse is unbounded and is defined only for data satisfying the corresponding square-summability condition on the inverse-weighted SVD coefficients. The projections and inverse formulas above cannot then be used on arbitrary data.

For convolution operators Φf=f⋆h\Phi f = f\star hΦf=f⋆h, the spectral formula gives

9.3.2 Tikhonov Regularization¶

Regularized inverse.

For an ill-conditioned operator, applying the unregularized inverse to noisy data can be unstable, since

Φ+y=Φ+Φf0+Φ+w=f0++Φ+wwheref0+:=Projker⁡(Φ)⊥(f0),\Phi^+ y = \Phi^+\Phi f_0 + \Phi^+ w = f_0^+ + \Phi^+ w \quad \text{where} \quad f_0^+ \mathrel{:=}\mathop{\mathrm{Proj}}_{\ker(\Phi)^\bot}(f_0),Φ+y=Φ+Φf0​+Φ+w=f0+​+Φ+wwheref0+​:=Projker(Φ)⊥​(f0​),

It reaches ∣ ⁣∣w∣ ⁣∣/σR|\!| w |\!|/\sigma_R∣∣w∣∣/σR​ when w∝uRw \propto u_Rw∝uR​, so a small singular value produces a large amplification factor 1/σR1/\sigma_R1/σR​. ∣μλ(σ)∣⩽Cλ<+∞andlim⁡λ→0μλ(σ)=1σ.|\mu_\lambda(\sigma)| \leqslant C_\lambda< +\infty \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{\lambda\rightarrow 0} \mu_\lambda(\sigma) = \frac{1}{\sigma}.∣μλ​(σ)∣⩽Cλ​<+∞andλ→0lim​μλ​(σ)=σ1​.

Larger source orders β⩽2\beta\leqslant 2β⩽2 therefore give faster convergence as ∣ ⁣∣w∣ ⁣∣|\!| w |\!|∣∣w∣∣ tends to zero. The rate in Theorem 9.4 saturates: choosing β>2\beta> 2β>2 gives the same general worst-case rate as β=2\beta=2β=2. The best rate obtainable in this way is

∣ ⁣∣fλ−f0∣ ⁣∣=O(ρ13δ23).|\!| f_\lambda- f_0 |\!| = O( \rho^{\frac{1}{3}} \delta^{\frac{2}{3}} ).∣∣fλ​−f0​∣∣=O(ρ31​δ32​).

The capped inverse in Figure 9.2, left, avoids this finite-order saturation, whereas Tikhonov regularization is limited to source orders β⩽2\beta\leqslant 2β⩽2. Quadratic regularization is easier to implement: its variational formulation leads to a linear system and does not require an SVD.

For compact operators with nonclosed range, no uniform linear rate follows over these source balls from finite-order source conditions alone. Linear rates are possible in finite dimension with a fixed smallest positive singular value, or under different structural assumptions, such as those used for sparse ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1 regularization in Chapter 10.

9.4 Quadratic Regularization¶

We now turn from infinite-dimensional recovery theory to numerical methods in finite dimension.

Convex regularization.

As in (9.9), we reconstruct a high-resolution image f0∈RNf_0 \in \mathbb{R}^Nf0​∈RN from noisy measurements y=Φf0+w∈RPy = \Phi f_0 + w \in \mathbb{R}^Py=Φf0​+w∈RP by minimizing a convex regularized objective:

fλ∈argminf∈RN    E(f):=12∣ ⁣∣y−Φf∣ ⁣∣2+λJ(f)(9.17)f_\lambda\in \underset{ f \in \mathbb{R}^N }{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\;\; \mathcal{E}(f) \mathrel{:=}\frac{1}{2} |\!| y-\Phi f |\!|^2 + \lambda J(f) \tag{9.17}fλ​∈f∈RNargmin​E(f):=21​∣∣y−Φf∣∣2+λJ(f)(9.17)

Here ∣ ⁣∣y−Φf∣ ⁣∣2|\!| y-\Phi f |\!|^2∣∣y−Φf∣∣2 measures data fidelity, with ∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣|\!| \cdot |\!|∣∣⋅∣∣ denoting the ℓ2\ell^2ℓ2 norm on RP\mathbb{R}^PRP, and J(f)J(f)J(f) is a convex penalty on RN\mathbb{R}^NRN.

The regularization parameter λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 balances these two terms and can be difficult to choose in practice. In simulations with a known reference signal f0f_0f0​, the parameter can be calibrated by minimizing the reconstruction error ∣ ⁣∣f0−f~∣ ⁣∣|\!| f_0-\tilde f |\!|∣∣f0​−f~​∣∣. Such a reference is generally unavailable in applications.

For noiseless data, w=0w = 0w=0, we study small values of λ\lambdaλ. As λ→0\lambda\rightarrow 0λ→0, minimizers of (9.17) approach solutions of a constrained problem under the assumptions below.

We may assume y∈Im(Φ)y \in \mathop{\mathrm{Im}}(\Phi)y∈Im(Φ) without changing the minimizers, since orthogonality gives

∣ ⁣∣y−Φf∣ ⁣∣2=∣ ⁣∣y−ProjIm(Φ)(y)∣ ⁣∣2+∣ ⁣∣ProjIm(Φ)(y)−Φf∣ ⁣∣2|\!| y-\Phi f |\!|^2 = |\!| y-\mathop{\mathrm{Proj}}_{\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}(\Phi)}(y) |\!|^2 + |\!| \mathop{\mathrm{Proj}}_{\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}(\Phi)}(y)-\Phi f |\!|^2∣∣y−Φf∣∣2=∣∣y−ProjIm(Φ)​(y)∣∣2+∣∣ProjIm(Φ)​(y)−Φf∣∣2

The first term is independent of fff, so replacing yyy by ProjIm(Φ)(y)\mathop{\mathrm{Proj}}_{\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}(\Phi)}(y)ProjIm(Φ)​(y) in (9.17) changes only an additive constant.

Let us recall that a function JJJ is coercive if

lim⁡∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣→+∞J(f)=+∞\lim_{|\!| f |\!| \rightarrow +\infty} J(f) = +\infty∣∣f∣∣→+∞lim​J(f)=+∞

i.e.

∀ K∈R,  ∃R>0,∣ ⁣∣f∣ ⁣∣⩾R⟹J(f)⩾K.\forall \,K\in\mathbb{R},\;\exists R>0,\quad|\!| f |\!|\geqslant R\quad\Longrightarrow\quad J(f)\geqslant K.∀K∈R,∃R>0,∣∣f∣∣⩾R⟹J(f)⩾K.

Assume that J:RN→RJ:\mathbb{R}^N\to\mathbb{R}J:RN→R is lower semicontinuous and coercive and that y∈Im(Φ)y\in\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}(\Phi)y∈Im(Φ). For each λ\lambdaλ, let fλf_\lambdafλ​ solve (9.17). The family (fλ)λ(f_\lambda)_\lambda(fλ​)λ​ is bounded, and every accumulation point f⋆f^\starf⋆ as λ↓0\lambda\downarrow0λ↓0 solves

f⋆∈argminf∈RN  {J(f)  ;  Φf=y}.(9.18)f^\star \in \underset{f \in \mathbb{R}^N}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; \left\{ J(f) \;;\; \Phi f = y \right\} . \tag{9.18}f⋆∈f∈RNargmin​{J(f);Φf=y}.(9.18)

Choose a convergent subsequence fλk→f⋆f_{\lambda_k} \rightarrow f^\starfλk​​→f⋆ as k→+∞k \rightarrow +\inftyk→+∞. Write m=inf⁡J>−∞m=\inf J> -\inftym=infJ>−∞. Full coercivity of JJJ can be replaced by boundedness of joint sublevel sets of J(f)J(f)J(f) and ∣ ⁣∣Φf∣ ⁣∣|\!| \Phi f |\!|∣∣Φf∣∣. The simplest prior functionals are quadratic, and can be written as

Example of convolution.

Consider the convolution operator

Φf=h⋆f,(9.22)\Phi f = h \star f, \tag{9.22}Φf=h⋆f,(9.22)

f^λ,m=h^m∗y^m∣h^m∣2−λd^2,m,(9.23)\hat f_{\lambda,m} = \frac{\hat h_m^* \hat y_m}{|\hat h_m|^2 - \lambda\hat d_{2,m}}, \tag{9.23}f^​λ,m​=∣h^m​∣2−λd^2,m​h^m∗​y^​m​​,(9.23)

9.4.1 Solving Linear Systems¶

If Φ\PhiΦ and LLL are not simultaneously diagonalizable in the required bases, the coefficient formula (9.21) is unavailable. We instead solve (9.20), written as

Af=bwhereA:=Φ∗Φ+λLandb=Φ∗y.A f = b \quad \text{where} \quad A \mathrel{:=}\Phi^* \Phi + \lambda L \quad \text{and} \quad b = \Phi^* y.Af=bwhereA:=Φ∗Φ+λLandb=Φ∗y.

For moderate NNN, up to a few thousand, direct methods solve this system at a cost of O(N3)O(N^3)O(N3) for a generic AAA. Since AAA is symmetric positive definite, Cholesky factorization A=BB∗A=BB^*A=BB∗ is a natural choice, with BBB lower triangular. Reordering the rows and columns can help preserve sparsity in the factors of AAA.

For large NNN, iterative solvers access AAA only through matrix-vector products. In imaging, operator structure often makes these products much cheaper than a dense O(N2)O(N^2)O(N2) computation. For a sufficiently sparse matrix AAA, the cost is typically O(N)O(N)O(N).

When AAA is symmetric positive definite, as assumed here, the conjugate gradient method solves the equivalent quadratic minimization problem

min⁡f∈RN  E(f):=Q(f):=12⟨Af, f⟩−⟨f, b⟩(9.24)\underset{f \in \mathbb{R}^N}{\min}\; \mathcal{E}(f) \mathrel{:=}\mathcal{Q}(f) \mathrel{:=}\frac12\langle A f,\,f\rangle - \langle f,\,b\rangle \tag{9.24}f∈RNmin​E(f):=Q(f):=21​⟨Af,f⟩−⟨f,b⟩(9.24)

This objective agrees with (9.17) up to a constant. Starting from any f(0)f^{(0)}f(0), conjugate gradients computes f(ℓ+1)f^{(\ell+1)}f(ℓ+1) by minimizing over the affine space generated by all gradients obtained so far, rather than taking a single gradient step as in Section 19.1:

f(ℓ+1):=argminf  {E(f)  ;  f∈f(ℓ)+Span(∇E(f(0)),…,∇E(fℓ))}.f^{(\ell+1)} \mathrel{:=}\underset{f}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; \left\{ \mathcal{E}(f) \;;\; f \in f^{(\ell)} + \mathop{\mathrm{Span}}(\nabla \mathcal{E}(f^{(0)}), \ldots,\nabla \mathcal{E}(f^{\ell}) ) \right\} .f(ℓ+1):=fargmin​{E(f);f∈f(ℓ)+Span(∇E(f(0)),…,∇E(fℓ))}.

This subspace minimization requires only one matrix-vector product per iteration. For ℓ⩾1\ell\geqslant 1ℓ⩾1, with initialization d(0)=∇E(f(0))=Af(0)−bd^{(0)} = \nabla \mathcal{E}(f^{(0)}) = Af^{(0)}-bd(0)=∇E(f(0))=Af(0)−b, the recurrence is

f(ℓ+1)=f(ℓ)−τℓd(ℓ)whered(ℓ)=g(ℓ)+∣ ⁣∣g(ℓ)∣ ⁣∣2∣ ⁣∣g(ℓ−1)∣ ⁣∣2d(ℓ−1)andτℓ=⟨g(ℓ), d(ℓ)⟩⟨Ad(ℓ), d(ℓ)⟩(9.25)f^{(\ell+1)} = f^{(\ell)} - \tau_\ell d^{(\ell)} \quad \text{where} \quad d^{(\ell)} = g^{(\ell)} + \frac{ |\!| g^{(\ell)} |\!|^2 }{ |\!| g^{(\ell-1)} |\!|^2 } d^{(\ell-1)} \quad \text{and} \quad \tau_\ell = \frac{ \langle g^{(\ell)} ,\,d^{(\ell)}\rangle }{ \langle A d^{(\ell)},\,d^{(\ell)}\rangle } \tag{9.25}f(ℓ+1)=f(ℓ)−τℓ​d(ℓ)whered(ℓ)=g(ℓ)+∣∣g(ℓ−1)∣∣2∣∣g(ℓ)∣∣2​d(ℓ−1)andτℓ​=⟨Ad(ℓ),d(ℓ)⟩⟨g(ℓ),d(ℓ)⟩​(9.25)

where g(ℓ):=∇E(f(ℓ))=Af(ℓ)−bg^{(\ell)}\mathrel{:=}\nabla\mathcal{E}(f^{(\ell)})=Af^{(\ell)}-bg(ℓ):=∇E(f(ℓ))=Af(ℓ)−b. The iteration stops as soon as g(ℓ)=0g^{(\ell)}=0g(ℓ)=0.

It can also be shown that the directions d(ℓ)d^{(\ell)}d(ℓ) are AAA-orthogonal (conjugate), so that after at most NNN iterations in exact arithmetic, the conjugate gradient method computes the unique solution f(ℓ)f^{(\ell)}f(ℓ) of the linear system Af=bA f = bAf=b. In practice, it is usually used as an approximate solver, with far fewer than NNN iterations.

Nonlinear conjugate-gradient methods extend this idea to smooth objectives, but require a line search and additional safeguards. The linear-system step-size formula and finite-termination property above do not carry over unchanged.

9.5 Non-Quadratic Regularization¶

9.5.1 Total Variation Regularization¶

Quadratic regularization (9.19) often produces a blurred reconstruction fλf_\lambdafλ​. This can poorly approximate a signal f0f_0f0​ with sharp transitions, such as image edges.

In the convolutional case (9.23), the restoration operator is a filter, which tends to smooth sharp features.

For the squared-norm penalty, the restored signal belongs to ker⁡(Φ)⊥\ker(\Phi)^\botker(Φ)⊥, so missing components cannot be recovered. This statement does not hold for every quadratic penalty: a different matrix LLL can couple observed and unobserved components. Nonquadratic priors, particularly nonsmooth ones such as TV and ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1, encode structures such as edges and sparse coefficients that quadratic penalties do not model well.

Total variation.

Total variation is a widely used nonquadratic, nonsmooth prior. For smooth functions f:Rd↦Rf : \mathbb{R}^d \mapsto \mathbb{R}f:Rd↦R, it replaces the Sobolev or Dirichlet energy

JSob(f):=12∫Rd∣ ⁣∣∇f∣ ⁣∣Rd2dx,J_{\text{Sob}}(f) \mathrel{:=}\frac{1}{2} \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |\!| \nabla f |\!|_{\mathbb{R}^d}^2 \mathrm{d}x,JSob​(f):=21​∫Rd​∣∣∇f∣∣Rd2​dx,

where ∇f(x)=(∂x1f(x),…,∂xdf(x))⊤\nabla f(x) = (\partial_{x_1} f(x), \ldots, \partial_{x_d} f(x))^\top∇f(x)=(∂x1​​f(x),…,∂xd​​f(x))⊤ is the gradient, by the (vectorial) L1L^1L1 norm of the gradient

JTV(f):=∫Rd∣ ⁣∣∇f∣ ⁣∣Rddx.J_{\text{TV}}(f) \mathrel{:=}\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |\!| \nabla f |\!|_{\mathbb{R}^d} \mathrm{d}x.JTV​(f):=∫Rd​∣∣∇f∣∣Rd​dx.

Section 8.1.1 gives further background on these priors.

Removing the square 2^22 from the integrand changes which functions have finite energy.

For a nontrivial bounded set Ω\OmegaΩ with a smooth boundary, JSob(1Ω)=+∞J_{\text{Sob}}(1_\Omega)=+\inftyJSob​(1Ω​)=+∞, whereas JTV(1Ω)=Per⁡(Ω)<+∞J_{\text{TV}}(1_\Omega)=\operatorname{Per}(\Omega)<+\inftyJTV​(1Ω​)=Per(Ω)<+∞. More generally, an integrable function fff is of bounded variation when its distributional gradient DfDfDf is a finite vector-valued Radon measure. Its total variation is

JTV(f)=∣Df∣(Rd)=sup⁡h∈Cc1(Rd;Rd)∣∣h∣∣∞⩽1∫Rdf(x)divh(x) dx.J_{\text{TV}}(f)=|Df|(\mathbb{R}^d) =\sup_{\substack{h\in\mathcal{C}_c^1(\mathbb{R}^d;\mathbb{R}^d)\\ |\!| h |\!|_\infty\leqslant 1}} \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}f(x)\mathop{\mathrm{div}}h(x)\,\mathrm{d}x.JTV​(f)=∣Df∣(Rd)=h∈Cc1​(Rd;Rd)∣∣h∣∣∞​⩽1​sup​∫Rd​f(x)divh(x)dx.

For a finite vector measure mmm, its total mass is equivalently

∣m∣(Rd)=sup⁡h∈Cc(Rd;Rd)∣∣h∣∣∞⩽1∫Rd⟨h,dm⟩.|m|(\mathbb{R}^d)=\sup_{\substack{h\in\mathcal{C}_c(\mathbb{R}^d;\mathbb{R}^d)\\ |\!| h |\!|_\infty\leqslant 1}} \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\langle h,\mathrm{d}m\rangle.∣m∣(Rd)=h∈Cc​(Rd;Rd)∣∣h∣∣∞​⩽1​sup​∫Rd​⟨h,dm⟩.

The coarea formula for f∈BV(Rd)f\in\mathrm{BV}(\mathbb{R}^d)f∈BV(Rd) reads

JTV(f)=∫RPer⁡({f>t}) dt.J_{\text{TV}}(f)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\operatorname{Per}(\{f>t\})\,\mathrm{d}t.JTV​(f)=∫R​Per({f>t})dt.

For smooth functions, this agrees, for almost every level, with integrating the (d−1)(d-1)(d−1)-dimensional Hausdorff measure of the level sets. For general BV functions, superlevel-set perimeters, rather than measures of the pointwise sets {f=t}\{f=t\}{f=t}, are required.

Discretized Total variation.

For discrete data f∈RNf \in \mathbb{R}^Nf∈RN, the construction in Section 8.1.2 generalizes (8.6) to any spatial dimension:

JTV(f)=∑n∣ ⁣∣∇fn∣ ⁣∣RdJ_{\text{TV}}(f) = \sum_n |\!| \nabla f_n |\!|_{\mathbb{R}^d}JTV​(f)=n∑​∣∣∇fn​∣∣Rd​

∀ u∈Rd,∣ ⁣∣u∣ ⁣∣ε:=ε2+∣ ⁣∣u∣ ⁣∣2.\forall \,u \in \mathbb{R}^d, \quad |\!| u |\!|_\varepsilon\mathrel{:=}\sqrt{ \varepsilon^2 + |\!| u |\!|^2 }.∀u∈Rd,∣∣u∣∣ε​:=ε2+∣∣u∣∣2​.

The resulting regularized inverse problem (9.17) thus reads

fλ:=argminf∈RN  E(f)=12∣ ⁣∣y−Φf∣ ⁣∣2+λJTVε(f)(9.26)f_\lambda\mathrel{:=}\underset{f \in \mathbb{R}^N}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; \mathcal{E}(f) = \frac{1}{2}|\!| y-\Phi f |\!|^2 + \lambda J_{\text{TV}}^\varepsilon(f) \tag{9.26}fλ​:=f∈RNargmin​E(f)=21​∣∣y−Φf∣∣2+λJTVε​(f)(9.26)

9.5.2 Gradient Descent Method¶

The optimization program (9.26) is an example of smooth unconstrained convex optimization of the form

min⁡f∈RN  E(f)(9.27)\underset{f \in \mathbb{R}^N}{\min}\; \mathcal{E}(f) \tag{9.27}f∈RNmin​E(f)(9.27)

where E:RN→R\mathcal{E}: \mathbb{R}^N \rightarrow \mathbb{R}E:RN→R is a C1\mathcal{C}^1C1 function. Recall that the gradient ∇E:RN↦RN\nabla \mathcal{E}: \mathbb{R}^N \mapsto \mathbb{R}^N∇E:RN↦RN of this functional (not to be confused with the discretized gradient ∇f∈RN×d\nabla f \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times d}∇f∈RN×d of fff) is defined by the following first-order relation

E(f+r)=E(f)+⟨∇E(f), r⟩RN+o(∣ ⁣∣r∣ ⁣∣RN)\mathcal{E}(f+r) = \mathcal{E}(f) + \langle \nabla\mathcal{E}(f),\,r\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^N} + o(|\!| r |\!|_{\mathbb{R}^N})E(f+r)=E(f)+⟨∇E(f),r⟩RN​+o(∣∣r∣∣RN​)

A locally Lipschitz gradient improves the remainder to O(∣ ⁣∣r∣ ⁣∣2)O(|\!| r |\!|^2)O(∣∣r∣∣2). Mere continuity of the gradient does not give this stronger estimate.

For such a function, the gradient descent algorithm is defined as

f(ℓ+1):=f(ℓ)−τℓ∇E(f(ℓ)),(9.28)f^{(\ell+1)} \mathrel{:=}f^{(\ell)} - \tau_\ell \nabla \mathcal{E}( f^{(\ell)} ), \tag{9.28}f(ℓ+1):=f(ℓ)−τℓ​∇E(f(ℓ)),(9.28)

The step size τℓ>0\tau_\ell>0τℓ​>0 must balance stability against progress per iteration.

Section 19.1 analyzes convergence and explains how it depends on the step size τℓ\tau_\ellτℓ​.

9.5.3 Examples of Gradient Computation¶

Note that the gradient of a quadratic function Q(f)\mathcal{Q}(f)Q(f) of the form (9.24) reads

∇Q(f)=Af−b.\nabla \mathcal{Q}(f) = Af-b.∇Q(f)=Af−b.

In particular, the first-order optimality condition ∇Q(f)=0\nabla \mathcal{Q}(f)=0∇Q(f)=0 is equivalent to the linear system Af=bAf=bAf=b.

For the quadratic fidelity term G(f)=12∣ ⁣∣Φf−y∣ ⁣∣2\mathcal{G}(f)=\frac{1}{2}|\!| \Phi f-y |\!|^2G(f)=21​∣∣Φf−y∣∣2, one thus obtains

∇G(f)=Φ∗(Φf−y).\nabla \mathcal{G}(f) = \Phi^*(\Phi f - y).∇G(f)=Φ∗(Φf−y).

In the special case of the regularized TV problem (9.26), the gradient of E\mathcal{E}E reads

∇E(f)=Φ∗(Φf−y)+λ∇JTVε(f).\nabla \mathcal{E}(f) = \Phi^*(\Phi f - y) + \lambda\nabla J_{\text{TV}}^\varepsilon(f).∇E(f)=Φ∗(Φf−y)+λ∇JTVε​(f).

For differentiable maps F:RP→R\mathcal{F}:\mathbb{R}^P\to\mathbb{R}F:RP→R and H:RN→RP\mathcal{H}:\mathbb{R}^N\to\mathbb{R}^PH:RN→RP, the chain rule gives

∇(F∘H)(f)=DH(f)∗∇F(H(f)).\nabla(\mathcal{F}\circ\mathcal{H})(f)=D\mathcal{H}(f)^*\nabla\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{H}(f)).∇(F∘H)(f)=DH(f)∗∇F(H(f)).

Apply it to JTVε=∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣1,ε∘∇J_{\text{TV}}^\varepsilon=|\!| \cdot |\!|_{1,\varepsilon}\circ\nablaJTVε​=∣∣⋅∣∣1,ε​∘∇, where ∣ ⁣∣u∣ ⁣∣1,ε=∑nε2+∣ ⁣∣un∣ ⁣∣2|\!| u |\!|_{1,\varepsilon}=\sum_n\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+|\!| u_n |\!|^2}∣∣u∣∣1,ε​=∑n​ε2+∣∣un​∣∣2​. The result is

∇JTVε(f)=∇∗Nε(∇f)=−div(Nε(∇f)),Nε(u)n=unε2+∣ ⁣∣un∣ ⁣∣2.\nabla J_{\text{TV}}^\varepsilon(f)=\nabla^*\mathcal{N}^\varepsilon(\nabla f) =-\mathop{\mathrm{div}}(\mathcal{N}^\varepsilon(\nabla f)), \qquad \mathcal{N}^\varepsilon(u)_n=\frac{u_n}{\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+|\!| u_n |\!|^2}}.∇JTVε​(f)=∇∗Nε(∇f)=−div(Nε(∇f)),Nε(u)n​=ε2+∣∣un​∣∣2​un​​.

Thus the gradient of the energy is computed by taking finite differences, normalizing the resulting vector field, and applying minus the divergence.

Since div=−∇∗\mathop{\mathrm{div}}=-\nabla^*div=−∇∗, their operator norms are equal. For unscaled forward differences in ddd dimensions with periodic boundaries, ∣ ⁣∣∇∣ ⁣∣op⩽2d|\!| \nabla |\!|_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant 2\sqrt d∣∣∇∣∣op​⩽2d​. The Hessian of u↦ε2+∣ ⁣∣u∣ ⁣∣2u\mapsto\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+|\!| u |\!|^2}u↦ε2+∣∣u∣∣2​ is

Iddε2+∣ ⁣∣u∣ ⁣∣2−uu∗(ε2+∣ ⁣∣u∣ ⁣∣2)3/2,\frac{\mathrm{Id}_d}{\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+|\!| u |\!|^2}} -\frac{uu^*}{(\varepsilon^2+|\!| u |\!|^2)^{3/2}},ε2+∣∣u∣∣2​Idd​​−(ε2+∣∣u∣∣2)3/2uu∗​,

and is bounded above by ε−1Idd\varepsilon^{-1}\mathrm{Id}_dε−1Idd​. Consequently, a Lipschitz constant for the gradient of E\mathcal{E}E is

L=∣ ⁣∣Φ∣ ⁣∣op2+λ∣ ⁣∣∇∣ ⁣∣op2ε.L=|\!| \Phi |\!|_{\mathrm{op}}^2+ \frac{\lambda|\!| \nabla |\!|_{\mathrm{op}}^2}{\varepsilon}.L=∣∣Φ∣∣op2​+ελ∣∣∇∣∣op2​​.

The smallest eigenvalue of this pointwise Hessian is ε2/(ε2+∣ ⁣∣u∣ ⁣∣2)3/2\varepsilon^2/(\varepsilon^2+|\!| u |\!|^2)^{3/2}ε2/(ε2+∣∣u∣∣2)3/2, which tends to zero as ∣ ⁣∣u∣ ⁣∣→∞|\!| u |\!|\to\infty∣∣u∣∣→∞. Thus smoothed TV is not globally strongly convex. If Φ\PhiΦ is injective, the fidelity term supplies a global strong-convexity constant σmin⁡(Φ)2\sigma_{\min}(\Phi)^2σmin​(Φ)2; otherwise additional analysis on bounded sublevel sets is needed.

A fixed step 0<τ<2/L0<\tau<2/L0<τ<2/L gives convergence of gradient descent when a minimizer exists. As ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow0ε↓0, this bound forces small steps, motivating the nonsmooth methods developed in later chapters. A modest positive ε\varepsilonε can also reduce the staircase artifacts of exact TV regularization.

9.6 Examples of Inverse Problems¶

We now discuss several inverse problems in imaging that can be solved using quadratic regularization or nonlinear TV.

9.6.1 Deconvolution¶

The blurring operator (9.1) is diagonal in the Fourier domain, so quadratic regularization can be solved efficiently using fast Fourier transforms under periodic boundary conditions. We refer to (9.22) and the corresponding explanations. TV regularization does not reduce to a single diagonal Fourier solve and requires an iterative optimization algorithm.

9.6.2 Inpainting¶

For the inpainting problem, the operator defined in (9.2) is diagonal in space

Φ=diagm(δΩc[m]),\Phi = \mathop{\mathrm{diag}}_m( \delta_{\Omega^c}[m] ),Φ=diagm​(δΩc​[m]),

and is an orthogonal projector Φ∗=Φ\Phi^* = \PhiΦ∗=Φ.

For noiseless data, we enforce the affine constraint {f∈RN  ;  y=Φf}\left\{ f \in \mathbb{R}^N \;;\; y=\Phi f \right\}{f∈RN;y=Φf} using the orthogonal projector

∀ x,Py(f)(x)={f(x)ifx∈Ω,  y(x)ifx∉Ω.\forall \,x, \quad P_y(f)(x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} f(x) \quad \text{if} \quad x \in \Omega,\\ \; y(x) \quad \quad \text{if} \quad x \notin \Omega. \end{array} \right.∀x,Py​(f)(x)={f(x)ifx∈Ω,y(x)ifx∈/Ω.​

Projected gradient descent solves (9.18) for a smooth prior. For the Sobolev energy, the algorithm iterates

f(ℓ+1)=Py(f(ℓ)+τΔf(ℓ)).f^{(\ell+1)}= P_y( f^{(\ell)} + \tau \Delta f^{(\ell)} ).f(ℓ+1)=Py​(f(ℓ)+τΔf(ℓ)).

The iteration converges if 0<τ<1/40<\tau<1/40<τ<1/4, since ∣ ⁣∣Δ∣ ⁣∣⩽8|\!| \Delta |\!|\leqslant 8∣∣Δ∣∣⩽8. Figure 9.4 shows how it progressively fills the missing region.

Figure 9.4. Sobolev projected gradient descent algorithm.

Figure 9.5 illustrates Sobolev inpainting on a flower image with a known grid-shaped occlusion.

Figure 9.5. Sobolev inpainting of a grid-shaped occlusion on the flower image.

For the smoothed TV prior, the gradient descent reads

f(ℓ+1)=Py(f(ℓ)+τdiv(∇f(ℓ)ε2+∣ ⁣∣∇f(ℓ)∣ ⁣∣2))f^{(\ell+1)}= P_y\left( f^{(\ell)} + \tau \mathop{\mathrm{div}}\left( \frac{ \nabla f^{(\ell)}}{ \sqrt{\varepsilon^2+|\!| \nabla f^{(\ell)} |\!|^2} } \right) \right)f(ℓ+1)=Py​(f(ℓ)+τdiv(ε2+∣∣∇f(ℓ)∣∣2​∇f(ℓ)​))

which converges if 0<τ<ε/40<\tau<\varepsilon/40<τ<ε/4.

Figure 9.6 compares Sobolev and TV inpainting on the same observed flower pixels. The displayed reconstructions illustrate their different treatment of smooth regions and edges; their SNR values are measured against the same clean image.

Figure 9.6. Inpainting with Sobolev and TV regularization.

9.6.3 Tomography Inversion¶

In an idealized two-dimensional tomography model, each projection integrates the unknown image along a line Δt,θ\Delta_{t,\theta}Δt,θ​ defined by

x⋅τθ=x1cos⁡θ+x2sin⁡θ=tx \cdot \tau_\theta = x_1 \cos\theta+ x_2\sin\theta= tx⋅τθ​=x1​cosθ+x2​sinθ=t

Here τθ=(cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)\tau_\theta=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)τθ​=(cosθ,sinθ) is the unit normal to the line.

The resulting Radon transform is

∀ θ∈[0,π),∀ t∈R,pθ(t)=∫Δt,θf(x) ds=∬f(x) δ(x⋅τθ−t) dx\forall \,\theta\in [0,\pi), \forall \,t \in \mathbb{R}, \quad p_{\theta}(t) = \int_{\Delta_{t,\theta}} f(x) \,d s = \iint f(x)\, \delta( x \cdot \tau_\theta - t )\, d x∀θ∈[0,π),∀t∈R,pθ​(t)=∫Δt,θ​​f(x)ds=∬f(x)δ(x⋅τθ​−t)dx

see Figure 9.7.
